reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Jake had a cold. He had to blow his nose a lot. His tissues piled up on his bed.

Mom brought a small bin. She put it by his shoe on the floor. "Look," she said. She dropped one tissue in. Plunk!

Jake sat up. Could he do that too? He picked up a tissue. He held it up high. He let it go. It fell into the bin. Plunk!

Jake giggled. He found another tissue. This one was a little shy of the bin. It missed and landed on his shoe. Jake picked it up. He moved closer to the bin. He dropped it in. Plunk!

One tissue was stuck to his blanket. He pulled it off. He dropped it in. Plunk! Now the bed was all clean. The bin was full of tissues.

Jake clapped. "Look, Mom! All fixed!"

Mom smiled. "Nice work," she said. Then she held up one more tissue. "Can you do it again?"

Jake reached out his hand. "Drop it!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. Mom gave him a big pencil and pink paper.

"I will write my name!" said Gabriel.

He held the pencil in his fist. He made a G. It came out wobbly. He made an A. It fell over like a sleepy cat. Gabriel frowned. His name looked wrong.

Mom put a pink eraser on the table. "Try this," she said.

Gabriel rubbed the eraser on the wobbly G. He looked close. The mark was gone! The paper was clean again.

"Again!" said Gabriel.

He rubbed out the sleepy A too. Then he held the pencil with his fingers, the way Mom showed him. He wrote G. It stood up tall. He wrote A. It sat up straight.

Gabriel jumped from his chair. He ran to the woman washing dishes at the sink.

"Look, Grandma! I wrote Gabriel!"

Grandma held the paper up high. "My clever boy!" she said.

Gabriel looked at his name on the pink paper. He smiled big. "I want to write it ten more times!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Bennett sat on the yellow rug in the music room. Miss Rosa played a song on her drum. "Clap along," she said.

Bennett clapped fast, fast, fast. His hands went everywhere. The claps did not match the drum at all. His friend Milo put his hands in his lap. "Too tricky," said Milo.

Miss Rosa played the drum again. Boom. Boom. Boom. Bennett closed his eyes and listened. He waited. Then he clapped one time with each boom. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. His claps landed right on the beat. "I did it!" he said. He took Milo's hands. "Listen first," said Bennett. "Then clap." They clapped together, boom by boom.

Then they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" from memory. Miss Rosa hid her paper with the words, just to see. The boys sang every word. She gave them each a cup of milk. Bennett took a big drink and clapped one more time, boom.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Oliver sat at the dinner table. He wanted his peas to be a rocket ship. "Can peas fly?" he asked. "Let's try," said Dad.

Dad put ten peas on Oliver's plate. Brown bread sat beside them. Oliver pointed at each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad said that was good counting.

"Now we go down," said Dad. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six." Oliver ate one pea each time. "Five, four, three, two, one." One pea was left. "Blast off!" said Oliver. He popped it in his mouth and jumped up from his chair.

"What was that?" Oliver asked. "A countdown," said Dad. "Again!" said Oliver. Dad fetched more peas, one by one, until the bowl was empty.

"Ten, nine, eight," said Oliver slowly. He waited between each pea. "Seven, six, five." Mom clapped her hands. "Four, three, two, one. Blast off!" The last pea went up, up, into Oliver's mouth.

Dad laughed. "My rocket boy," he said. "Bedtime countdown next. Ten, nine, eight..." Oliver giggled all the way down to one.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Evan wanted to sort his things in the backyard. He made three piles. One pile for animals. One pile for toys. One pile for foods.

First he put the apples in the food pile. "One apple, two apples," he said. Then he put the banana there too. The food pile was growing.

Next came the animals. A ladybug landed on a leaf. "Animal," said Evan. He heard a bird sing. "Animal," he said again. He watched a squirrel run up the tree. "Animal," he said, and laughed.

Then he held his favorite stuffed dog. It was brown and soft. He set it in the animal pile. He looked at the squirrel. It ran and jumped. He looked at his stuffed dog. It just sat there. It did not eat. It did not bark. It was not alive. Evan picked it up and put it in the toy pile, next to his red ball. "One toy, two toys," he said.

His dad came out with a snack. "Nice sorting," Dad said. "Can I ride my toy truck too?" Evan asked. Dad smiled. "After your snack," he said. Evan bit the apple and waved it at the toy pile.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Isabelle went to the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to find a gift for Mama. "Let us look," said Grandpa. They walked past the cows. Isabelle saw a shiny red apple in the basket. She picked it up.

"Now close your eyes," said Grandpa. Isabelle closed her eyes. "What do you hear?" "A duck," she said. She heard the duck quack. "Good. Ears hear," said Grandpa.

Then Grandpa held up a lemon. "Taste this," he said. Isabelle licked it. Her mouth went tight. "Sour!" she said. Then she licked a strawberry. "Sweet!" she said. "My tongue knows." Grandpa laughed.

Isabelle sniffed the hay. "Nose smells," she said. She touched the soft lamb. "Hands feel." She looked at the shiny apple. "Eyes see." She put the apple in her bag. At home, Mama bit the apple. "Sweet," said Mama. Isabelle clapped her hands. "My tongue said so first," she said. Mama gave her a strawberry from the bowl.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Josephine wanted the big red fire truck. It sat inside a big box on the shelf. The box looked fun. Maybe more trucks were hiding in there.

Josephine pulled the box. It did not move. She pulled again. Still no. The box was heavy. "Oof," she said. She sat down on the rug to wait and think. Her teacher came over. "Want some help?" she asked. "Yes please," said Josephine. Together they pulled one more time. Slowly, the box slid down. It made a big bump on the rug.

Inside was a soft yellow pillow. Josephine picked it up. Up it came, so easy! The pillow was light. She hugged it and carried it fast across the room. Then she walked back slow, so the pillow would not fall. Her friend Ben patted the pillow. "Soft," he said. Josephine kissed the pillow, right on the corner. "My light pillow," she said. "My big truck can ride on top." She set the red fire truck on the pillow and marched around the rug, holding it high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Alexis sat at the big table. His friend Sam from school came for dinner. Alexis had his red car in his pocket.

After the food, Alexis put the car on the table. He pushed it fast. Vroom, vroom. Sam watched. Sam reached out his hand.

Alexis held the car tight. His tummy felt tight too. He wanted to grab it away. But then he sat still. He took one slow breath. Then two. Then three. His tummy felt soft again.

"You can have a turn," Alexis said. He gave Sam the car. Sam pushed it across the table. The wheels made a little sound. Sam laughed. Alexis laughed too.

"Watch this," said Sam. He rolled the car to Alexis. It bumped his cup. Alexis picked it up. It was his turn again. He washed his hands first, because they were sticky, and then he rolled the car back to Sam.

Daddy set down a plate of warm bread. It smelled good. Mom touched Alexis's ear gently and smiled at him.

"My turn, your turn," said Alexis. He rolled the car one more time, all the way across the tablecloth.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jacob stood in the bathroom. Mom ran the bath water. Jacob put his hand near the faucet. "Hot water is for me to turn," said Mom. Jacob watched her feel the water. "Just right now," she said.

Jacob took off his socks. His toes touched the warm floor. He heard the water splash. He heard the tub fill up. Then he sniffed. He sniffed again. "Mom! I smell spaghetti!" "Yes," said Mom. "Dad is cooking it now." Jacob had not seen the spaghetti. But his nose knew first. He liked that.

Jacob got in the tub. The warm water touched his legs. He splashed with his hands. "Don't miss your ears," said Mom. She washed behind them. Then she dried him with his big furry towel. It was soft on his cheeks. Dad called from the kitchen, "Dinner, little man!" Jacob sniffed the air one more time and grinned. "Spaghetti time!"

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Ivy went to the library on a hot summer day. She wanted to draw on the big tablet there. But the screen was dark. She poked it. Nothing happened. She tapped it with two fingers. Still nothing.

A librarian named Sam walked by. "Try the little round button," Sam said, "on the side." Ivy found it. She pressed the button. The screen woke up. Ivy pressed it again, and the screen went dark. She pressed it one more time. The screen woke up again. "On and off, like a light," said Sam, laughing.

Ivy opened the drawing app. She drew a cat with a purple hat. Then she drew a dog with a pancake. When she was done, she remembered the little button. She pressed it, and the screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf.

"Bye, dark screen," said Ivy.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Jaxon marched into the living room. The big game was on TV. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Uncle Ben was there too. Jaxon climbed onto the soft couch and clapped his hands.

"Go, go, go!" Jaxon shouted. One team wore red shirts. One team wore blue shirts. The red team ran and ran. They ran so fast! The blue team ran slowly, like a turtle. Then the blue team kicked the ball. It went into the net! The blue team got a point. Later, the blue team kicked it in again. Two points for blue!

The game ended. The whistle blew. "Red ran more," said Jaxon. "Red wins!" Uncle Ben laughed. "Look at the numbers," he said. He pointed to the big screen. The score said blue had two. Red had one. Blue had more points. Blue won the game. Blue got the shiny gold cup.

Jaxon clapped and jumped up and down. "Blue has more points! Blue wins!" Grandma gave him a hug. Dad put a red hat on Jaxon's head. "Maybe next time," said Dad. Jaxon grinned and shouted, "Let's watch one more game!"

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Ezra went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought warm bread, fresh butter, and a big carton of milk. "Can I have toast here?" Ezra asked. "Yes," said Dad. "I will teach you to make it."

Dad got bread and butter from the bread stand. He held the hot toast himself. Then he gave Ezra a small knife. Ezra spread the butter. He made it flat and smooth. "I did it!" said Ezra. "Now milk," said Ezra.

Ezra tried the big milk carton. It was too heavy. Milk nearly spilled. Dad saw Ezra's face. He poured some milk into a little jug. Ezra picked up the little jug. It was light in his hands. He tipped it slowly. Milk went into the cup. Not one drop spilled. Ezra took a sip. "Dad, was the big carton too big for me?" "Yes, little jug, little hands," said Dad. Ezra grinned and poured himself some more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Leah went to the library with her mom. She wanted a book about dogs. Where would a dog book hide?

Leah saw a shelf with a sign. The sign said "Animals." She found books with cats, elephants, and dogs. She patted the dog on the cover. "Hello, dog," she said.

Next to her, a boy named Sam was playing with blocks. He put all the red blocks in one pile. "Red here," he said. Then Sam laughed. He mixed them up. He put all the big blocks in one pile instead. The same blocks, but in a new way!

Leah looked at the shelves again. The animal books were all together. But she saw something new. On another shelf, books stood in a rainbow. Red books, then yellow books, then green books. Same books, different shelves!

"Mom, look," said Leah. "The books moved!" Mom smiled. "Someone sorted them by color today."

Leah picked her dog book. It was blue. She held it up to the blue shelf. "You belong here," she said, "but you come home with me."

At the desk, the librarian let Leah stamp the book. Thump went the stamp, right on the page. Leah touched her nose to the dog's nose on the cover. "Good dog," she whispered.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Sienna sat at the craft table at summer camp. She wanted to make a paper sun. The sun needed lots of yellow strips.

"Can I use the big scissors?" Sienna asked. Ms. Rosa held up a small pair instead. "These are your safety scissors," she said. "They have rounded tips. I will watch you cut."

Sienna held the little scissors. Snip, snip, snip. A yellow strip fell down. Then another one. "Look, my sun is getting rays!" she said.

Then she saw something funny. Each snip made a strip fall. Snip, strip. Snip, strip. "It's raining paper!" said her friend Tom. He put out his bag to catch them.

One strip landed on Tom's head. "Now you have a yellow hat!" said Sienna. Tom laughed and shook it off. It fell into the bag.

"My hands are all dirty with glue," said Sienna. She wiped them on a wet cloth. Then she glued the strips around a yellow circle. Her paper sun was done.

Ms. Rosa hung it in the window. The real sun shone right through it. "Two suns!" said Tom. Sienna giggled and pointed. "Mine has better rays. Snip, snip!"

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Jasper wanted to find his red ball. It was not on the shelf. It was not under the rug. That was a problem.

Jasper looked at the toy box. It was full of blocks. It was full of dolls too. He could not fit one more thing. "I guess I will make room," he said.

Jasper picked up a block. "You are a toy," he said. He set it on the shelf. He picked up a doll. "You are a toy too." He set it by the block. Soon the box had room. He peeked inside. There was the red ball, hiding at the bottom!

Jasper gave the ball a gentle pat. His little sister came in. She could not reach her doll. Jasper picked up the doll and handed it to her. She smiled big.

"Ball?" she said, pointing.

"Yes," said Jasper. "Let's roll it together."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Lea sat at the big art table. She was making a paper crown. It had red stars and yellow dots.

"I will wear it home," said Lea.

First, one star. Second, one dot. Third, another star. She spread the wet glue. It felt cold and sticky on her fingers. It smelled like flour and water.

Teacher Mia sat close by. "Take your time," she said.

Lea wanted to try the crown on. She picked it up too soon. The stars slid. The dots slid too. The pieces came apart in her hands. Lea's lip wobbled. "My crown is broken," she said.

Teacher Mia knelt down. "It is not broken. Wet glue needs to dry," she said. "Let's set it flat and wait."

They laid the crown on the table. Lea counted the pieces. One, two, three, four. Then they watched the glue. It went from shiny to dull. Lea touched one star. It held!

Lea pressed the crown on her head. It stayed. It felt like a real queen's crown.

"My crown is full of stars," said Lea. "And it will not slide off!"

Teacher Mia smiled. "You made it all by yourself," she said.

Lea walked to the cubbies, crown shining, and held Teacher Mia's hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ellie sat at the big table. Grandma put warm bread in a basket. Grandpa held up his hands. Everyone got quiet.

"Who will say the bread words?" Grandma asked.

Ellie wanted to say them. She had practiced at home. She had practiced in the bath. "Me! Me!" said Ellie. Grandpa smiled. "Let's hear it, Ellie."

Ellie stood on her chair. "Sit down, sweet pea," said Grandma. "Feet on the floor." Ellie sat down. Then she said the words. "Hamotzi." Everyone said "Amen" together. Grandpa clapped. The bread basket went around and around.

After dinner, Uncle Ben showed Ellie his plate. It was empty. Hers was different. She still had bread on it. "Look," said Uncle Ben. "Your words started the meal. Then we ate it all up." Ellie looked at her bread. She took a big bite. Then everyone laughed. Ellie laughed too. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. "Again tomorrow," said Grandpa.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Sofia sat in the family car with her toy bunny. "Are we going to the doctor?" she asked. "The doctor checks my whole body!"

Mama smiled and drove fast. "We will hurry," said Mama. "We have a special visit today."

The car stopped at a new place. Sofia saw a big tooth on the door. A big tooth! She held her bunny tight.

Inside, a friendly woman said, "Hello! I am the dentist."

"A dentist?" said Sofia.

"The dentist is a doctor for teeth," the woman said with a smile.

Sofia opened her mouth wide, wide, wide. The dentist looked and looked. She counted Sofia's teeth. Then she gave Sofia a shiny sticker.

"A tooth sticker!" said Sofia. It was her favorite kind of surprise.

Bunny got a check too. "Open up, bunny," said Sofia. The dentist clapped. "Perfect teeth," she said.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Rehmat wanted to play the shouting game with her big brother. He said one word. She had to shout the opposite word back.

"Ice cream is cold," said her brother. Rehmat thought and thought. "Then soup is hot!" she shouted. Her brother laughed and clapped.

Next he ran around the playroom, fast as a rabbit. Rehmat crawled like a sleepy turtle. "Slow," she said. Her brother nodded. "Fast and slow are opposites too."

Then Rehmat got it wrong. He said "big," and she said "big" back. Her brother shook his head. Rehmat felt grumpy. Her mouth turned down. She hugged her teddy.

Mama came in and sat on the floor. "Try again," said Mama softly. Rehmat looked at the teddy. Then she looked at her brother. He was big. The teddy was small.

"Small!" Rehmat shouted. Her brother pointed at her and cheered. "You got it!"

Rehmat giggled. She held up the teddy. "Big bear," she said. Then she squished it tiny. "Small bear!" Her brother laughed. Mama clapped her hands.

Rehmat snuggled between Mama and her brother. She whispered one more word to the teddy. "Soft," she said. Then she poked her brother's elbow. "Hard!"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to bake cookies for his family. Grandma said, "Let's make them together."

Parker helped mix the dough. He poured the sugar. He dropped in the blue bowl of chocolate chips. Some chips fell on the floor, and Grandma smiled and helped him pick them up.

The dough was ready. Grandma put the pan in the hot oven. Parker wanted to look inside. He reached for the oven door. Grandma said, "Stop. That is hot. A grown-up opens the oven." Parker stepped back and waited.

While they waited, Parker watched a bird fly past the window. The bird landed in its nest in the big tree. Parker sat very still so he would not scare it.

Then Grandma said, "The cookies are done." She put on her big mitts. She opened the oven door. The cookies looked golden and warm. Parker saw that Grandma always touched the hot oven, and he never did. He got to carry the plate to the table instead.

The family ate the cookies. Dad said, "These are the best cookies ever." Parker grinned and said, "Can we ride home with some for tomorrow?"

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Weston was in the backyard. He had a big pot and a wooden spoon. He wanted to make soup for his bear, Ted.

He found three pinecones. He put them in the pot. He poured in some water from the hose. Then he began to stir. "Soup is ready!" he said.

Weston lifted the spoon to his mouth. He wanted a big slurp. Just then Mom came out. "Stop, Weston," she said. "Pretend soup is for pretending." Weston looked at his spoon. The water was cold and muddy. He put the spoon down.

He sat on the square patio stone. He was sorry he almost ate it. "Let's pretend to slurp instead," said Mom. She sat down too. They slurped and slurped with empty spoons. Ted got a pretend drink too. Weston smiled. "More soup, please!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Nova sat at the long wooden table. Big bowls of soup sat in the middle. Everyone held hands. Nova did not know what came next.

Grandma squeezed Nova's hand. Grandma began to speak. She thanked the sun and the farmers and the soup. Nova waited. She wanted to eat, but she kept holding hands. When would the talking end?

Then Grandma said one word. "Amen." Everyone let go of hands. Everyone picked up spoons. Nova blinked. The waiting word meant the food could start.

The next week, Nova came back to the hall. She brought a small present for Grandma. It was a drawing of soup. Everyone held hands again. Nova listened hard. Grandma thanked the sun and the farmers. Nova waited and waited.

"Amen," said Grandma.

Nova laughed and grabbed her spoon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Everett was four today. The whole family drove to Grandma's house. Grandpa blew up red balloons. One balloon popped and Everett jumped. Then he laughed.

"Time for cake," said Grandma. She lit the candles with a match. Everett watched from far away. The candles glowed. "Make a wish," said Grandma. Everett closed his eyes. He wished hard. Then he blew and blew. The little flames went out. Everyone clapped.

Then the singing began. "Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday dear..." Everett waited. Would they say his name? "Everett!" they sang. His very own name, right in the song. He hid his face in his hands. He was not mad. He was smiling a big smile. His cheeks felt warm. "Sing it again," he said. So they did. "Happy birthday dear Everett!" And he smiled behind his hands one more time.

story:
Elijah stood by the cubbies at school. He pulled off his shoes. Then he pulled off his socks. He put them in his cubby. After snack time, he came back. He looked inside. He saw one tiny sock. Just one.

"Where is the other one?" said Elijah. MissAna knelt down beside him. "A sock needs its partner," she said. "Two socks make a pair." Elijah looked under the bench. He saw a red horse toy. He saw a crayon. No sock.

Elijah began to sing the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." He walked slowly along the wall. "Six, seven, eight." He looked at the little toy shelf. "Nine, ten." He froze. There, behind a tiny chair, was his sock!

Elijah picked it up. He held the two socks together. One sock, then the other sock. A pair! He put them on his feet. They were warm and soft. Then he ran to the rug. "Look, Miss Ana!" he said. "One for this foot. One for that foot!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Bennett ran in from Grandma's backyard. He had been spinning in circles under the big tree. His head felt dizzy and his shoes were full of grass.

"Grandma, I want to cook!" he said. Grandma was mixing pancake batter in a blue bowl. The batter smelled like vanilla and warm mornings.

"First, the sink," said Grandma. She pointed with her wooden spoon. Bennett looked at his hands. They had dirt on them. He turned the faucet. The water ran cool over his fingers. He rubbed the soap until white bubbles grew. He rinsed the bubbles away. Now his hands were clean.

Then Grandma let him stir. Round and round went the spoon. The flour and milk turned into smooth batter. "Look," said Bennett. "I made it change!"

Grandma cooked the pancakes on the hot stove. Bennett stood far back and watched. Soon the pancakes came to the table. They were golden and soft.

Bennett took a big bite. Then he felt something small in his pocket. He pulled out a tiny pinecone from the backyard. Grandma laughed. "That one is not for eating," she said. Bennett giggled and put it in the middle of the table, next to the syrup.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
It was a big day for Audrey. Mom said, "Today we get your shot!" Audrey held Mom's hand. They walked into the pharmacy together.

A nurse smiled. "Hello, Audrey! Sit up here on the big table." Audrey climbed up. The table was tall and cold. She felt her tummy go tight. She wanted to hop right down.

Then Mom sat on a chair. Mom opened her arms wide. "Come sit on my lap," said Mom. Audrey slid down and snuggled in. Mom held her close, like a deep, warm hug. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Quick! The shot was done!

"Was that it?" asked Audrey. She looked at her arm. There was a tiny pink bandage. The nurse poured a spoon of sweet syrup as a treat. Audrey drank it all up. "That was easy!" she said. Mom laughed and swung her high. On the way out, Audrey waved to the nurse. "See you next time!" she called.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Peyton was at Grandma's house. She sat at the big table in the sunny room. Grandma put out red paint and a fat brush.

"I will paint a fish," said Peyton. She dipped the brush in the red paint. She painted a wiggly fish on the paper. Then she ran outside to see the dog.

The brush stayed in the paint cup all night. In the morning, Peyton picked it up. The brush was stiff. The bristles were hard and stuck together. "Oh no," said Peyton. She touched the brush. It would not bend.

Grandma brought a cup of water. Peyton dipped the stiff brush in. She swished it round and round. The water turned pink. The brush got soft again. The bristles were clean and fresh.

Peyton painted a new fish. This time she rinsed the brush right away. She put it on a towel to dry. "Good helper," said Grandma. Peyton smiled and painted one more fish, a big red one.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jaxson sat at the dinner table. He had a big idea. He would bang his drum after eating!

"Can I play my drum?" he asked.

"Yes, after dinner," said Mom.

Jaxson was so excited. He ate fast. Then he got his drum. BOOM! BOOM! He danced in his chair. What a happy boy!

Then he heard a sound. It was a little cry. His baby sister was covering her ears. Her doll fell on the floor. Her face looked sad, then scared.

"Hmm," said Jaxson. "I love the drum. But she does not."

Dad picked up the baby. "She likes quiet sounds," he said.

Jaxson put the drum down. He picked up her doll. He made the doll dance, slow and soft. The baby stopped crying. She smiled. She clapped her hands.

Jaxson smiled too. Loud for him. Quiet for her. Two people, one table, two different feelings.

"More doll dance!" said Jaxson. The doll spun around and around.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Rowan went to the big cultural center with Mom. The room was full of red and gold. Lanterns hung from the ceiling. They gave off a warm light.

Rowan saw his cousin Mei. Mei held a small red envelope. It was shiny and flat. Rowan wanted one too. He looked and looked. "Where is mine?" he asked.

Grandpa came over with a smile. He put a red envelope in Rowan's hand. Rowan wanted to open it fast. He pulled at the corner. Then he saw Mei. Mei bowed to her grandma first. She said, "Thank you." Only then did she open her envelope.

Rowan stopped pulling. He looked up at Grandpa. "Thank you," he said. Grandpa laughed and patted his head. Rowan opened his envelope. There was money inside! A shiny coin slid out into his palm. Rowan held it up to the lantern light. "Mei, look!" he said. Mei clapped her hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Audrey sat on a small red chair. She had a pencil and some paper. She wanted to write the letter K. Her name had a K in it, but she could not write it yet.

She tried once. The lines went the wrong way. She tried again. It still looked funny. Her pencil got stuck on the paper. Audrey felt sad. Then she saw a box of bumpy letter cards. She picked out the K card. The letter was big and rough. She put her finger on the card. She traced the top line down. She traced the little lines out. Her arm moved slowly, again and again.

Then Audrey picked up her pencil. She drew the lines on her paper. It was a K! Audrey smiled. "I can write my name," she said. She wrote the K one more time, very big, right in the middle of the page.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Sadie ran to the bike at the playground. She wanted to ride it right away. She put her foot on the pedal.

Her grandma held up a helmet. "Sadie, come here first," she said. Sadie ran back. Grandma put the helmet on her head. It felt hard and smooth. The strap clicked under her chin.

Then Sadie rode the bike. She pedaled past the swings. Her nose picked up the smell of popcorn. A man was making popcorn in a hot pot. Grandma stood by him, but Sadie stayed back. The pot was far too hot to touch. Grandma carried the popcorn over in a paper bag. It was warm and good.

Sadie rode one more time around the path. Then her front wheel hit a small rock. The bike tipped. Sadie fell onto the soft ground. Bonk went her helmet on the path. Sadie sat still for a short minute. Then she stood up.

She touched her helmet with one hand. It had a little mark on it. "My head is okay," she said. She turned the bike upright. "One more ride," said Sadie. Grandma smiled and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Aubrey went to the computer lab with her class. The teacher said, "Today we learn tablets." Aubrey wanted to draw a cat on the screen. She had never done it before.

First she pressed the round button. The screen lit up. She pressed it again and the screen went dark. "Oops," said Aubrey. She pressed it one more time. Light again! Then the teacher helped her find the drawing app. Aubrey tapped it open. She mixed blue and yellow on the screen. Green! She drew one cat, two cats, three cats. "Meow," she said to each one.

Then it was time to go. Aubrey ran to the little couch and set the tablet down on the soft cushion. Ben came running to sit. "Wait!" said the teacher. She picked up the tablet just in time. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place," she said. Aubrey looked at the shelf. It had a green tag with her name.

Aubrey carried the tablet back. One, two, three, she counted the steps to the shelf. She set it on the green tag. It fit just right. "Good night, tablet," said Aubrey. The teacher smiled. "Happy tablet, happy shelf," she said. Aubrey waved at her three cats through the dark screen.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Alexander stood in the sunny kitchen. He wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. Mom said the water was getting hot.

Alexander stepped close to the stove. The pot made a cloud of steam. The steam felt hot on his face. He jumped back fast.

"Ouch," he said. "That is very hot."

Mom picked him up. "Watch from here," she said. She set him on a chair far from the stove. Alexander held his pencil. He drew the pot and the bubbles on his paper.

The steam went up and up. The water went bump, bump, bump. Alexander saw that the steam came from the hot pot. When the pot got hot, the steam came out.

Mom made the noodles. She gave Alexander a bowl. He clapped his hands. Then he took a big bite.

"Hot pot, good noodles," he said. Mom laughed and gave him more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Josephine ran straight to the library story room. Her friends Ben and Mia were there. "Let's play hide-and-seek!" said Ben.

"I will count," said Josephine. "You hide!" Ben and Mia ran to hide behind the big book shelf. Josephine counted, "One, two, three!" She counted very fast. Then she turned around. Ben and Mia were still standing in the open!

"You counted too fast!" said Mia. "We need time to hide."

"Okay," said Josephine. "I will count slow." Ben and Mia ran off again. Josephine counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She counted slowly, like a song.

Now Ben and Mia were gone. Josephine looked behind the shelf. Not there. She looked under the table. Not there. Then she heard a giggle by the coat rack. "I see you, Mia!" said Josephine. "Look at you, hiding behind the coats!"

Mia laughed and laughed. "You counted slow," she said. "So we got to hide!"

"Who wants to count next?" asked Josephine.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Julia stood by the big piano in the band room. She wanted to make a song. Her teacher, Mr. Bell, smiled at her. "Try the keys," he said.

Julia looked at the keys. Some were black. Some were white. She tapped a white key. It made a low sound. She tapped another white key. It made a new sound. Then she tapped a black key. That one made a sound too. She thought only white keys could play. But the black keys played!

Julia pressed only the black keys. One, then two, then three. The sounds went up and down. "It sounds like raindrops!" she said. A boy named Sam was upset because his drum was too big for him. Julia said, "Listen to my rain song." Sam stopped frowning. He tapped his drum very softly along with her.

Mr. Bell gave them both a thumbs up. Julia played her black keys again. Sam tapped his drum again. "Let's give our song a name," said Julia. Sam said, "Rain and Drum!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Grandpa had a big red dog named Bess. "B is for Bess!" said Grandpa. Evan wanted to read her name all by himself.

Grandpa wrote DOG on paper. Evan looked hard. "Bog!" he said. Then he laughed and laughed. "Bess is a bog!"

"No, no," said Evan again. He looked closer. The first letter had a round part. Which way did it face? He made his own fist. He turned it left. He turned it right. The round part of the b faced the same way as his right hand. The d faced the other way! "D, d, dog!" Evan shouted. "It says dog!"

Grandpa clapped. A shy gray cat ran under the chair. A feather floated down from Bess's tail. Evan picked it up. He held it like a pen.

"Now I can write too," said Evan. He climbed onto the tall stool. He drew a big D. Then a little d. Then the round part faced the wrong way, so he fixed it. "D is for dog," he said. "D is for door. D is for Grandpa's donuts!"

Bess barked one big bark. Evan laughed. "B is for Bess. B, b, bark!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Matthew saw a big blue bus. It was full of books. "This is the bookmobile," said Mommy. "You can get your own library card today."

Matthew got a little white card. It had his name on it. He smiled and smiled. He picked a book about a red fire truck. "I want this one," he said.

The librarian put the book in a bag. Then Matthew saw a small slot in the side of the bus. A girl was standing by it. She held her book tight. "I don't want to let it go," she said. Her daddy held her hand. "Wave it goodbye," he said. The girl waved the book. Then she dropped it into the slot. It went in and made a soft sound. "Bye, book," she said. "See you soon."

At home, Matthew read the fire truck book three times. Mommy sang a little song about it. His tooth felt loose when he smiled big.

One week later, the bookmobile came back. Matthew ran to the bus. He held his fire truck book tight too. Then he remembered the girl. He waved his book. "Bye, book," he said. He dropped it into the slot. The librarian smiled. "Here is a new card for you," she said. It was a sticker of a fire truck.

"I did it all by myself," said Matthew.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Henry walked into his classroom. He held his dad's hand. His backpack felt heavy on his back. There were new toys on every table.

A boy stood by the blocks all alone. Henry wanted a friend to play with. But he did not know the boy's name.

Henry asked his dad, "What do I do?"

His dad said, "Go find out his name."

Henry took a big breath. He walked over to the blocks. "My name is Henry," he said. "What is your name?"

The boy smiled big. "I am Sam!" said Sam. "I like blocks. Do you?"

"Yes!" said Henry. They stacked the blocks up high. Then the tower fell down. Crash! Both boys laughed.

"Let's build a house," said Sam. "It can be a doctor's house. My mom is a doctor."

"Can I touch the doctor's door?" asked Henry.

"Only if you knock first," said Sam.

Henry knocked on the block door. Knock, knock. Sam opened it. "Hello, friend," said Sam.

"Hello," said Henry. He handed Sam one more block.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Myles sat at the little table in art class. The sun was sunny outside the window. His teacher put out paper and paints.

"I want to paint a boat," said Myles. "But I can't make the sail." He looked at the circle stamp. He looked at the square sponge. Neither one looked like a sail.

His friend Nia was eating her lunch. Her sandwich was cut into triangles. "Look," she said. She pointed at one piece. Myles counted the corners with his finger. One, two, three. Then he counted the sides. One, two, three. A triangle had three sides and three corners, just like a sail.

Myles found the scissors-safe sponge with three sides in the tray. He dipped it in white paint. He pressed it on his paper. There was a triangle sail. He pressed it again for the other sail.

He painted a square boat under the sails. He painted a rectangle flag on top. Then he hopped up to show his teacher.

"The sail has three corners," said Myles. He pointed at each one. His teacher smiled and hung the boat on the sunny wall.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The chair leaned back like a rocket ship. The dentist had shiny tools and a little cup of water with ice in it. "First we wash our hands," said the dentist, Miss Kim. Grace wanted to be a helper. But when she got to the sink, she scrubbed for two seconds and turned off the water. "That was fast," said Miss Kim. Grace looked at her hands. The germs could still hide in her soapy fingers, and germs made teeth and tummies sick.

At camp, Grace had learned a song for the sink. She began to sing it, soft and low. "Happy hands, scrub and rub, soap and bubbles, scrub and rub." She kept scrubbing while she sang. The bubbles turned white and fuzzy on her hands. The song was long. The scrubbing was long too. At last she rinsed, and the water carried the bubbles away. Her hands felt smooth and clean.

"Now I can be a helper," said Grace. Miss Kim gave her a fuzzy sticker shaped like a tooth. Grace stuck it on her shirt. She sang the song again on the way out, just because she liked it.
